title: Officer feared for life, coroner's inquest hears
article: Seconds before he was gunned down by Victoria police on the evening of Feb. 3, 2007, John Seguin made a fatal decision.

With two police vehicles in hot pursuit and police blocking off the narrow side street he had turned up, Mr. Seguin veered onto the boulevard and accelerated toward a veteran Victoria officer at full speed.
At a B.C. Coroner's inquest into Mr. Seguin's death, Sergeant John Ayers testified yesterday that he fired three shots directly at the oncoming vehicle, believing that his life was in danger.
"At that point, what I see is a set of headlights and 'GMC.' It's big enough and close enough that I could touch it," Sgt. Ayers told the five-person coroner's jury.
"I drew my weapon and fired three shots. The only option at that point in my mind was the handgun."
Sgt. Ayers, a 21-year veteran of the Victoria Police Department, then jumped out of the oncoming vehicle's path.
Officers who saw Sgt. Ayers fall back believed he had been hit.
Sgt. Mike Johnston, who was riding with Sgt. Ayers when the incident occurred, testified that he fired two shots as the vehicle accelerated down the boulevard.
Sgt. Johnston said he had a clear view of the driver as the vehicle passed him where he had retreated between some parked cars for safety.
"I fired two shots directly at the driver. I didn't fire at the vehicle, I fired at the driver," Sgt. Johnston said.
"Then I think to myself, 'Oh, my God, John Ayers is dead.' "
The driver, not identified as Mr. Seguin until after the incident, picked up speed, careering onto busy Hillside Avenue and then turning back toward the roadblock as bullets continued to fly.
At that point, a police cruiser broadsided the stolen Jimmy and sent it spinning into a nearby lamp standard, where it came to rest with the accelerator jammed open and its wheels spinning.
Sgt. Ayers then walked over and fired two rounds into the front left wheel in an attempt to disable the vehicle.
Seconds later, the engine stopped revving and officers determined the vehicle's occupant was seriously wounded.

In all, police fired 12 shots during the melee, which lasted "seven to 10 seconds," according to Sgt. Ayers. A forensic autopsy later determined that Mr. Seguin died from a single gunshot to the head.

Sharilyn Cadwallader, a former acquaintance of the victim, testified on Tuesday that Mr. Seguin, who had an extensive criminal history, was a heavy cocaine user and supported the expensive habit in part by stealing cars.
"When I drove in cars with him he would say, 'I'm warning you right now before you get in, this car is stolen and if we get in a police chase I'm not stopping,' " she said.
